young.html: George Berkeley was an Irish bishop with a surprising idea. Think about a table. You can see it, touch it, knock on it. But what is the table, apart from what you see and feel and hear? Berkeley said: nothing. For things like tables, to be is to be perceived.

That sounds strange! Does the table vanish when everyone leaves the room? Berkeley said no, because God always perceives everything. So the world is real and steady, but it is made of ideas in minds, not of some hidden "matter" behind them.

Berkeley liked a test with water. Make one hand warm and the other cold, then put both in the same bowl of lukewarm water. One hand says "cold!" and the other says "warm!" Which is right? Berkeley said heat and cold are in our feelings, not out in the water.

young.name: gb-water-hands
young.cap: Warm one hand and cool the other, then dip both in the same water. What does each hand feel?

young.html: The three-bowl test. With a grown-up, set out three bowls: cool water, lukewarm water and warm (not hot) tap water. Hold one hand in the cool bowl and one in the warm bowl for a minute, then put both into the lukewarm bowl. What does each hand tell you?

full.html: Berkeley (1685–1753) was 25 and a fellow of Trinity College, Dublin, when he published the Principles of Human Knowledge in 1710. He later became Bishop of Cloyne, spent three years in Rhode Island planning a college in Bermuda that never opened, and gave his library and farm to Yale. He wrote the Principles to answer skeptics and those who doubted God, and he expected his idea to bring philosophy back to common sense.

full.text: To be is to be perceived

full.html: Berkeley starts from Locke: what we know directly are ideas. Then he asks what it means to say a sensible thing exists:

full.text: The table I write on I say exists, that is, I see and feel it; and if I were out of my study I should say it existed—meaning thereby that if I was in my study I might perceive it, or that some other spirit actually does perceive it. There was an odour, that is, it was smelt; there was a sound, that is, it was heard; a colour or figure, and it was perceived by sight or touch.
full.author: George Berkeley
full.ed: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), Project Gutenberg text

full.text: For as to what is said of the absolute existence of unthinking things without any relation to their being perceived, that seems perfectly unintelligible. Their ESSE is PERCIPI, nor is it possible they should have any existence out of the minds or thinking things which perceive them.
full.author: George Berkeley
full.ed: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), Project Gutenberg text

full.html: Esse est percipi is Latin for "to be is to be perceived." Berkeley says this of sensible things. Minds, which he calls spirits, are different: their being is to perceive and to act.

Locke had said colors and tastes are only in us but shape and size are really in things. Berkeley replies that we can't even imagine a shape with no color, or a size apart from how it looks or feels. And shapes and sizes change with where we stand, just as colors change with the light. So if secondary qualities are only in the mind, primary ones are too. "Matter" as something unthinking, unseen and unfelt behind our ideas is, he says, an empty word.

full.name: gb-water-hands
full.cap: Berkeley's argument from the bowl of water: the same water can't be both warm and cold, so warmth must be in the feeling.

full.html: If tables are ideas, why can't I wish them away? Because, Berkeley answers, ideas of sense are not made by my will. They come in a steady, lawful order from another mind, God. What scientists call the laws of nature are the regular ways God gives us ideas. Science still works; it studies these regularities. What goes away, Berkeley says, is an unseen matter that explains nothing.

Thinking Berkeley said the world is a dream or that nothing is real. He said the opposite: the things we see and touch are real, and are exactly what they seem. What he denied was matter existing apart from all minds.

deep.html: Samuel Johnson, the subject of the Boswell rung, is said to have kicked a large stone and said, "I refute it thus." Berkeley's defenders say this misses the point: Berkeley never denied that stones feel solid. David Hume, the next rung, praised Berkeley's arguments but turned them in a skeptical direction, and Kant later tried to separate his own view from Berkeley's.

Berkeley is often called the founder of idealism, the view that reality is fundamentally mental. Most philosophers today don't accept his conclusion, but his questions about perception, what we can know of things apart from experience, are still argued over. His Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous (1713) present the same ideas in a livelier form and appear in the Harvard Classics readings.
